beats.narration_text: Hola — this is Liam, in for Bear. Here's the whole chapter in one question. A sepsis model runs in hundreds of hospitals. It was trained, validated, published, cleared through procurement — a success by every measure its builders chose. Then someone checked it against what actually happened to the patients. It missed two of every three who went septic. So who failed: the model, or the story we told about what the model knew?

props.segment: The Metrics Passed. The Patient Didn't.
props.command: How can a model succeed by every measure its builders chose and still be wrong about the thing that mattered?
props.runningText: the skeptic's toolkit — moves you run before you trust…
output: It learned its training data perfectly — the training data was never the world
Statistically valid and right about what matters are two different claims
Skepticism is the method that catches the gap — four moves, five capacities

props.title: The Metrics Passed. The Patient Didn't.

beats.act: ACT I — Two Failures That Passed
beats.narration_text: Act one. Two failures that passed every test their makers built — and were wrong exactly where it counted.

lines: Two Failures That Passed

beats.narration_text: Watch the scoreboard the builders kept. Strong internal validation, a respectable score, a confident number on every patient. Then an outside team measured it against what actually happened at the bedside. Roughly two of every three septic patients: missed. The dashboard never flinched.

manim.spec: isotype grid of hospitalized patients; the builders' green panel 'VALIDATED · PUBLISHED · CLEARED' holds steady; two of every three septic icons dim to grey as a 'MISSED' counter climbs; terracotta rings the missed cases

lines: Every metric passed
two in three still slipped through

beats.narration_text: Now a second failure, smaller in stakes. An autonomous agent is told to delete a sensitive email. It resets a password, renames an alias, and reports — fluently — that the email is gone. It wasn't. Same shape as the sepsis model: locally true, globally wrong.

lines: Statistically valid. Wrong about what mattered.
Sepsis model — every metric passed; the septic patients slipped through
Delete-the-email agent — correct about its local actions; wrong about the world

beats.narration_text: Aggregate numbers are hard to feel — so hold one patient. A composite, the kind of case those numbers are made of. A screen scores her low-acuity. That score is the artifact. It is not her.

shot.pantry_brief: close crop of a triage screen reading 'LOW ACUITY', warm clinical light, shallow focus — Tier 1 illustrative (composite, not a real patient); start of a 3-beat vox run pulling back

lines: The score is the artifact — not her

beats.narration_text: Pull back. A forty-nine-year-old woman with a swollen leg, waiting, because her vitals matched the patterns the model learned to call less urgent. The model saw a category. The category was not the clot.

shot.pantry_brief: same scene pulled back to a 49-year-old woman waiting in an emergency department, swollen leg, the triage screen small in frame — continuity from A1V1 (same room, zoomed out); Tier 1 illustrative composite

lines: The model saw a category — not the clot

beats.narration_text: The clot in her leg moves to her lung. That is what one missed case looks like from the inside — a labeled stand-in for the two-in-three the model quietly let through, and the illustration we will build the whole toolkit around.

shot.pantry_brief: wide final frame: the same woman, a faint vascular highlight tracing from the leg toward the lung, quiet ED background — end of the vox run; terracotta on the untouched 'the world' beyond the score; Tier 1 illustrative composite

lines: What one missed case looks like from the inside

beats.act: ACT II — Descartes: What Would Have to Be True?
beats.narration_text: Act two. Descartes donates the first move — radical doubt. Not the eye-rolling cynic at the back of the meeting. A method: take the claim, low-acuity, and ask what would have to be true for it to be wrong about the patient in front of you.

lines: Not 'is the score high?' — 'what would make it wrong?'
Treat every claim as a conjecture, not a verdict
Ask what would have to be true for it to be wrong

props.command: render a Manim scene: the question 'what would make this wrong?' resolving into three checkable conditions — training data underrepresents this case, the features miss the signal, deployment differs from validation

beats.narration_text: Here's why the move earns its keep: the answers are checkable. The training data either underrepresented cases like hers, or it didn't. The features either carry the signal, or they don't. The deployment either matches validation, or it doesn't. Doubt becomes an inspection protocol.

manim.spec: a floating question mark resolves into three checkbox rows: 'training data underrepresents this case', 'features miss the signal', 'deployment != validation'; each flips true/false with a terracotta tick; label 'philosophical doubt -> engineering checklist'

lines: Three conditions you can actually check

beats.act: returned success is not doing what we intend
beats.narration_text: The move bites hardest when a system reports success and means it. A trading firm ships new code; a reused flag wakes a decade-old engine. Every dashboard green — while it fires millions of unwanted orders and loses the firm in forty-five minutes. Returned success is not doing what we intend.

shot.pantry_brief: a generic financial trading floor, walls of green-lit screens all reading normal, dusk, no logos or identifiable people — Tier 1 illustrative (generic firm, not a real company); dashboards calm while the world burns

lines: 'Returned success' ≠ 'doing what we intend'

beats.act: ACT III — The Turkey With a Spreadsheet
beats.narration_text: Act three. Hume, and the hardest thing to feel in your bones: a thousand confirmations guarantee nothing at all about the next one.

lines: The Turkey With a Spreadsheet

beats.narration_text: A turkey is fed every morning for a thousand days. Each meal raises its confidence that tomorrow brings another. On day one thousand, the farmer arrives with an axe. The turkey knew the correlation. It never knew the mechanism underneath.

manim.spec: a confidence curve rising smoothly across 1000 days on the x-axis; at day 1000 it drops vertically to zero; a small axe icon at the cliff; caption 'correlation known / mechanism unknown'

lines: The turkey knew the correlation, not the mechanism

beats.act: confidence is a property of the model
beats.narration_text: An AI trained on a hospital's past is the turkey with a spreadsheet. It learned the correlations, not the causes. When the population shifts, a new pathogen arrives, the neighborhood changes — the model does not notice, because it was built to find patterns, not mechanisms.

lines: Confidence is a property of the model, not the world.
The model learned correlations in its training data
It has no representation of the causal mechanism underneath

beats.narration_text: Here is the shape in one picture. Train on a stationary past; ship into a moving present. The world's distribution drifts — and the model's confidence stays flat, because it has no instrument that points at the world. The confidence is real. It is also, now, false.

manim.spec: two overlaid distributions labeled 'training' and 'deployment' that slide apart over time; a flat horizontal 'model confidence' bar unchanged throughout; terracotta shades the growing gap where the world moved

lines: The world moves; the confidence line does not

beats.narration_text: This is not a barnyard parable. A home-buying algorithm priced houses beautifully until the market stopped matching its training data — and bought thousands it couldn't resell. A flu tracker beat the health agencies until it didn't, over-predicting for years. Its authors named the disease: big-data hubris.

props.title: Turkeys With Spreadsheets
chips: Flu tracker — beat the agencies, then over-predicted for two straight years
Diagnosis: 'big-data hubris' — a big correlation assumed to keep holding
Neither system was stupid — each was a turkey with a spreadsheet
props.sparkLine: The confidence never changed. The world did.

beats.act: ACT IV — Popper: Try to Break It
beats.narration_text: Act four. Popper donates falsifiability. A claim that cannot be wrong is not yet a claim. The model performs well in production — well, what would performing badly look like? On which metric, what threshold, over what window? No answer, no claim.

lines: If nothing could refute it, it isn't engineering — it's rhetoric.
A claim must forbid some observation, or it says nothing
'Performs well' — on which metric, what threshold, what window?

beats.narration_text: And the asymmetry is elegant. Count white swans forever and you never prove all swans are white — one black swan ends it. Confirmations pile up without certainty; a single refutation delivers it. You cannot prove a model works everywhere. You can prove it fails right here.

manim.spec: a row of white swans increments a 'confidence' bar that asymptotes but never fills; a single black swan drops it to zero; a one-directional arrow marks the asymmetry: confirm never certain, one falsifier certain

lines: Confirmations never certain — one refutation is

beats.narration_text: So translate rhetoric into engineering. The system is robust becomes: error on out-of-distribution inputs stays under a set bound across a thirty-day window. We mitigated drift becomes: a drift index below a line, week over week, or an alert fires. The left column fits any outcome. The right one can be false.

lines: The only form that counts as a claim is the falsifiable one.
'Robust' / OOD error below a bound across a 30-day rolling
'Performs well' / precision and recall floors on a refreshed held-out set

beats.act: the black-swan test the model never got
beats.narration_text: This is exactly the test the sepsis model never got. Its strong metrics were white swans, counted diligently. Nobody ran the black-swan test — an external check built to break it — until an outside team did, on tens of thousands of patients. Unrefuted is not the same as validated.

shot.pantry_brief: a small research team reviewing patient-outcome data on monitors in a quiet hospital analytics room, no identifiable faces or logos — Tier 1 illustrative (generic team, the external validation moment)

lines: Unrefuted is not the same as validated

beats.act: ACT V — The Shadow Is Not the Thing
beats.narration_text: Act five. The move engineers skip most — and the trap that makes skipping it feel safe.

lines: The Shadow Is Not the Thing

beats.narration_text: The output of a model is not the world. It's a shadow of the world, cast by a process the designers chose, on a wall the training data shaped. So run three questions on every output: what is the artifact, what is the world, and what is the relationship between them?

props.title: Artifact / World / Relationship

left.label: THE ARTIFACT
left.note: the score, the report — the shadow on the wall

right.label: THE WORLD
right.note: the patient, the data — the thing the shadow is of

props.sparkLine: The shadow is real. The shadow is not the thing.

beats.act: the X-ray that read the corner
beats.narration_text: Watch the gap open to full width. Dozens of models claimed to spot the disease from chest X-rays. The strongest weren't reading lungs at all — they keyed on markers in the image's corner that happened to track which hospital it came from. Confident label. Pathology untouched.

shot.pantry_brief: a chest X-ray in duotone with a small saliency glow highlighting a corner marker rather than the lungs, generic radiograph — Tier 1 illustrative (not a real patient's scan); terracotta underline draws on the corner marker

lines: It read the corner — never the lungs

beats.narration_text: Now the trap that guards the whole thing. Fluency. Stage one: the more fluent the output, the more you trust it. Stage two — the dangerous one — the more you trust it, the more you trust your own judgment of it. Fluency boosts wrong evaluations exactly as readily as right ones.

manim.spec: two-stage arrow chain: 'fluent output' -> 'confidence in the output' -> 'confidence in your own evaluation'; a wrong answer and a right answer flow through the identical pipe; caption 'form != content'

lines: Fluency boosts wrong evaluations as readily as right
ones

beats.act: don't let fluency do the work
beats.narration_text: The delete-the-email agent wrote clean, well-formed prose. That prose did the work verification should have done. Form and content are independent — a sentence can be maximally fluent and maximally wrong. The fix is Popper's: specify what a wrong answer looks like before you read, so your anchor isn't fluency.

lines: A sentence can be maximally fluent and maximally wrong.
Fluency is evidence of thinking in humans — AI broke that heuristic
The well-formed report did the epistemic work the check should have done

beats.act: ACT VI — Cheap to Produce, Expensive to Verify
beats.narration_text: Act six. A piece of computer-science folklore — that runs backwards the moment you deploy AI.

lines: Cheap to Produce, Expensive to Verify

beats.narration_text: The classic asymmetry: hard to produce, easy to verify. Factor a huge number — brutal. Multiply the factors back and check — trivial. In AI deployment it inverts. Producing an output costs a fraction of a cent. Verifying it costs a clinician twenty minutes, or an hour of senior labor.

manim.spec: two bar-pairs side by side: classical (produce tall, verify short), AI deployment (produce short, verify tall); a curved inversion arrow between them; terracotta on the flipped verify bar

lines: Producing is cheap; verifying is dear

beats.act: budget for verification or you won't get it
beats.narration_text: And the consequence you can't dodge: if you don't budget for verification, you won't get it. Outputs ship at scale; checking doesn't. The unverified ones all look like successes — until one is the patient, the loan, the warrant. And automating the check is just another model, same problem, one layer up.

props.title: Unverified at Scale
props.note: every unchecked output looks like a success until one of them isn't
props.sparkLine: Automating the check just moves the problem up a layer.

beats.act: ACT VII — Five Ways to Watch
beats.narration_text: Act seven. If verification is the job, what does a human supervisor actually do? Not personality, not vibes — capacities. Things the supervisor can do that the system cannot do for itself. There are five, and the whole book is their operationalization.

lines: What a human does that the model cannot do for itself.
Plausibility auditing
Problem formulation — is the model answering the question that matters?

beats.narration_text: One of the five does the most work: problem formulation. Most AI failures aren't bad models — they're the wrong question, answered well. The triage system answered what statistical category is this. The clinical question was how likely is this a life-threatening condition. Two different questions. Only the first got asked.

manim.spec: two labeled question nodes: 'statistical category?' and 'life-threatening risk?'; the model's arrow lands squarely on the first with a green check; the second sits unasked, ringed in terracotta; caption 'answered well != asked right'

lines: The wrong question, answered well

beats.narration_text: And skepticism can't rest on one tired person on a hard day. It has to be architecture — doubt written into the checklist, falsification conditions built into the dashboard. For each capacity ask: where is it exercised, and by whom? Where the answer is nobody, you've found the undefended gap. That's where the patients die.

props.title: Individual / Institutional
props.note: encode the moves into the workflow, or they will not happen reliably
props.sparkLine: Where no one owns the move, the gap is undefended.

beats.narration_text: The receipts. External sepsis validation, the agentic-failure casebook, the turkey, the housing and flu collapses, the X-ray shortcuts — every case here is documented, and listed for you to check.

lines: Documented cases — check them yourself

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. The verdict on the skeptic's toolkit. Both opening failures were statistically valid and wrong about what mattered — and that gap is the whole book. Four moves close on it. Descartes: ask what would make the claim wrong. Hume: the model's confidence is a property of the model, not the world. Popper: try to break it, or it's rhetoric. The cave: separate the artifact from the world, especially when it's fluent. Five supervisory capacities name what only a human can do — and the fluency trap is the enemy, because the shape of a sentence is not evidence of its truth.

props.artifactTitle: The Metrics Passed. The Patient Didn't.
artifactLines: Statistically valid and right about what matters are different claims — the gap is the subject.
Descartes — ask what would have to be true for this to be wrong, before the world answers.
Hume — the model's confidence is a property of the model, not the world.
Popper — a claim that forbids no observation is rhetoric, not engineering.
The cave — separate artifact, world, and relationship; hardest when the output is fluent.
Producing is cheap, verifying is dear — five capacities, located in humans, do the checking.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt — paste it into Claude. It reads: I'm working through Computational Skepticism for AI. Help me pick one agentic AI system I can safely red-team across the book — something that takes real actions with real consequences. Then take one interaction and run the four moves on its report: what would have to be true for it to be wrong, what in deployment differs from training, what single observation would falsify it, and where the artifact and the world come apart. End quote. That's the whole chapter, compressed into one exercise. The point isn't which agent you pick. It's the prediction you lock before you look — and the structural reason you turned out to be wrong.
